title: Adapting Credibility Assessment Interview Technique (CAIT) to Probe LLM Honesty
original_idea: Map CAIT/CBCA forensic criteria onto LLM output features. Build evaluation set of honest vs. deceptive responses. Test whether forensic criteria predict deception.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Moderate theory: if forensic criteria transfer to AI, it provides a low-cost screening layer. But the transfer from human deception detection to LLM output is speculative.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Mapping criteria and running classification tests is accessible. Requires reading forensic psychology literature but the implementation is simple text analysis. No model training needed.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-scoped: map criteria, build small evaluation set, run classification. The deliverable is clear (does CAIT predict LLM deception?). Feasible in 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: A 2025 study applied CBCA (Criteria-Based Content Analysis) to LLM outputs, specifically using ChatGPT to evaluate forensic interview transcripts against the 19-item CBCA framework. This showed LLMs cannot reliably replicate expert CBCA judgment. However, the proposed idea inverts this: instead of using LLMs to apply CBCA, it applies CAIT/CBCA forensic criteria to LLM outputs to detect LLM deception. This inverse application — using forensic deception detection tools as features for an LLM deception classifier — is novel. The cross-domain transfer from forensic psychology to AI deception detection in this direction has not been systematically explored.

evidence: Can a Large Language Model Judge a Child's Statement? A Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Human Experts in Credibility Assessment. Journal of Evidence-Based Social Work, 2025.
Decoding LLMs' Verbal Deception in Online Reviews. Decision Support Systems, 2025.
Evaluation of the Deception Detection Capabilities of LLMs. ACL 2025.
